sections.title: The product rule along a path
An operation that probability cannot describe

opening: We have seen that a computation can be described as a run of configurations, each produced from the last by a transition rule, and that a reversible computation keeps enough information for every step to be undone. These ideas were developed for classical machines. Quantum computing asks what changes when the machine itself is a quantum system.
opening_continuation: Classical computations, whether they follow fixed rules, explore several possibilities, or make random choices, share a common language of transitions. Quantum mechanics, the physical theory of systems such as single atoms, fits into the same language with one decisive difference: the alternative ways in which a computation can unfold can cancel one another instead of simply accumulating. This effect, called interference, has no classical counterpart, and it is the resource that quantum algorithms exploit. It is also fragile. A record of which alternative occurred, left anywhere, destroys it, which is why reversibility and the clearing of workspace matter so much in quantum computation. The rules of quantum mechanics for a single qubit are derived here from how transitions compose, three observations, and three stated assumptions; Chapter 4 adopts them as postulates.
